_about: The 13-test movement assessment (from classic v4.0). Text and options only — scoring is app/js/engine/assessment.js. Option values are stored in the user's answers: never rename a value.

tests.name: Direction screen A — repeated forward bends
tests.how: Stand and slowly bend forward as if touching your toes, return to standing. 10 slow reps. How do your symptoms behave across the reps?
tests.why: From your initiation assessment: direction preference decides which positions your plan emphasizes — and which it bans.

tests.name: Direction screen B — standing extension
tests.how: Stand, hands on the small of your back, gently arch backward. 5 slow reps, small range only. How do your symptoms respond?
tests.why: Extension worsening symptoms = extension-intolerant pattern: press-ups and prone lying come OUT of the plan. This reversed your own program once — it matters.

tests.name: Prone hip extension — firing order
tests.how: Face down, forehead on hands. Put one hand on the glute and one on the hamstring of the working leg. Slowly lift the straight leg ~6 inches. Which muscle fires FIRST? Repeat per side.
tests.why: Glute-first is the healthy order. Hamstring or low back firing first = glute inhibition — the back does the glutes’ job and complains about it.

tests.name: Single-leg glute bridge hold
tests.how: On your back, one foot flat, other leg straight. Lift the hips to a straight line and hold 10 seconds, 3 reps per side. How does each side hold up?
tests.why: Hamstring cramping or a dropping pelvis = the glute is not carrying its load on that side.

tests.name: Clamshell — where do you feel it?
tests.how: Side-lying, knees bent, feet together. Open the top knee 10 slow reps without the pelvis rolling back. Where is the work?
tests.why: Deep in the buttock = glute med. Front/side of the hip = TFL compensating — a classic imbalance signature.

tests.name: Thomas test — hip flexor length
tests.how: Sit on the edge of a sturdy table or bed. Hug one knee to your chest and lie back, letting the other leg hang. What does the hanging leg do? Repeat per side.
tests.why: A thigh that cannot rest flat = tight hip flexors (iliopsoas) — the front anchor of anterior pelvic tilt.

tests.name: Pelvic tilt — mirror check
tests.how: Stand side-on to a mirror in your normal stance, wearing something with a waistband. Where does the waistband point, and how deep is your low-back arch?
tests.why: Anterior pelvic tilt (lower-crossed pattern): tight hip flexors + tight low back in front, weak glutes + weak deep core behind. The plan attacks all four corners.
options: Waistband tips down in front, deep arch, belly out

tests.name: Straight-leg raise — active vs passive
tests.how: On your back: (1) actively lift one straight leg as high as you can. (2) Then use a towel around the foot and gently pull it higher. Compare the two heights — and note what you feel.
tests.why: Passive much higher than active = a control deficit, not short hamstrings. The fix is strength, not aggressive stretching — protective hamstrings should not be yanked on.
options: Sharp / electric tug behind the knee

tests.name: Prone hip internal rotation
tests.how: Face down, one knee bent 90° with the shin vertical. Let the foot drop OUTWARD slowly — that measures internal rotation. Estimate each side honestly.
tests.why: A common finding in one-sided back pain: one hip rotates far less than the other, often on the symptomatic side. A stiff hip makes the lumbar spine rotate instead.

tests.name: 90/90 hip switch
tests.how: Sit with both knees bent at 90°, feet wide. Slowly rotate both knees side to side like windshield wipers, 8 switches. How does it move?
tests.why: Catches rotation limits the prone test misses, and shows which side guards.

tests.name: Side plank endurance (from knees)
tests.how: Side plank from the knees, elbow under shoulder. Time each side until form breaks (hips drop or roll). Enter seconds.
tests.why: McGill’s endurance ratios: left and right side-bridge times should sit within ~10% of each other. A gap is a lateral stability deficit — and QL territory.

tests.name: Wall posture test
tests.how: Stand with your back to a wall, heels a few inches out. What touches without forcing: tailbone, mid-back, and the back of your head?
tests.why: Head not touching = forward-head posture; shoulders rolling forward off the wall = rounded shoulders. Together: upper-crossed syndrome — chin tucks, rows and face pulls are its direct counter.
options: Shoulders roll forward off the wall
Head won’t touch AND shoulders roll

tests.name: Weight-shift guarding check
tests.how: Bend forward slowly and do a shallow knee bend, like you normally would. Notice honestly: do you shift your weight to one side to avoid loading the other?
tests.why: Many people with one-sided pain unconsciously shift away from the sore side when bending. Guarding protects short-term and overloads the other side long-term — the plan adds extra work to the avoided side.
